subject: NimbusFinance private deploy — egress anchor & connectivity options (Peering / PrivateLink / S2S)
messages:
From: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@nimbusfinance.com>

Cc: Priya Singh <priya.singh@nimbusfinance.com>, CloudOps <cloudops@nimbusfinance.com>

Subject: Private deployment: connectivity options, egress IP stability requirement

Hi Jonas —

Thanks for taking this. We're evaluating Redwood Private and need help choosing the best connectivity pattern. High level constraints:
- All inference traffic must be allowed-listable by third-party processors (fixed egress IPs required).
- Traffic should avoid the public internet where possible (AWS backbone preferred).
- Minimize blast radius between our production VPC and non-prod.
- On-prem datacenter uses a Palo Alto firewall that currently expects IPsec S2S connections.
- We need SOC 2 evidence for flow logs and access controls.

Attached is a simple network diagram (nimbus-network-diagram-v1.png). Initial ask: pros/cons of VPC peering vs PrivateLink (interface endpoints) vs site-to-site VPN for this use case, and any hybrid recommendation that balances egress stability and operational simplicity.

Can you also call out cost or schedule implications for each option? We're on a tight procurement window.

Appreciate it —
Alex
CTO, Nimbus Finance

Attachments referenced: nimbus-network-diagram-v1.png (image/png)
From: Jonas Weber <jonas.weber@redwood.com>
To: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@nimbusfinance.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Private deployment: connectivity options, egress IP stability requirement

Alex —

Thanks for the diagram and the clear constraints. Quick summary up front, then specifics:

Executive summary (short):
- PrivateLink (interface endpoints) gives the strongest isolation for Redwood-managed endpoints (service stays off the public internet) and is easiest for allow-listing on a per-endpoint basis, but it does not by itself give you a single fixed egress IP for *all* outbound connections from your VPC.
- A Transit Gateway + centralized NAT (EIP-backed NAT appliances) provides a deterministic egress set of IPs and clean on-prem propagation and pairs well with S2S IPsec to your firewall.
- VPC Peering is low-latency and simple for same-account peering, but it exposes routing across CIDR ranges (bigger blast radius) and doesn't scale well for multi-account topologies; peering alone won't address your requirement to control egress IPs to third parties.
- Site-to-site VPN (IPsec) to on-prem is useful for persistent datacenter connectivity but has variable throughput/latency and requires careful HA design; it does provide the required compatibility with a Palo Alto device.

Recommended architecture (pattern we usually propose for this profile):
1) Create a central Transit Gateway in the AWS landing account. Attach: customer production VPC, Redwood Private VPC (where inference lives), and the Transit-GW-facing AWS-managed IPsec for on-prem.
2) Put an EIP-backed NAT fleet (or managed NAT gateway pair) in a central egress VPC attached to the Transit Gateway. These NAT EIPs become your allowlistable egress IPs for third parties.
3) Use VPC Interface Endpoints (PrivateLink) for Redwood control-plane and API traffic so calls to Redwood never traverse the public internet and are isolated per service.
4) For data-plane/model traffic between your prod VPC and Redwood Private VPC, use Transit Gateway routing rather than peering so you have central route controls and can apply security policies/flow logs in a single place.

Why this hybrid: PrivateLink prevents exposing RPC endpoints publicly; Transit Gateway + central NAT gives a set of stable egress IPs that your vendors can rely on and is compatible with policy-based S2S to your firewall. It combines the strength of isolation (PrivateLink) with the operational requirement of deterministic egress.

Costs and schedule notes:
- PrivateLink: per-hour + per-GB interface endpoint charges. Moderate cost but often acceptable for control-plane traffic. See attached redwood-privatelink-costs.xlsx for ballpark numbers.
- Transit Gateway + NAT EIPs: TGW attaches and per-hour data processing; NAT EIPs (or egress appliances) incur additional cost and operational overhead.
- S2S VPN to TGW: faster to stand up than Direct Connect; acceptable for pilot but consider Direct Connect for sustained high throughput.

I'll sketch a mutual action plan and timeline if you want to proceed (quick discovery -> pilot TGW + interface endpoints -> cutover). 30–45 day runway typical for production readiness depending on procurement.

I can set a technical deep-dive with our infra engineering team (Grace) and our security lead (Karthik) tomorrow. Proposed 45-minute slot?

Cheers,
Jonas Weber
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Thanks team — couple follow-ups:
- Our Palo Alto on-prem requires policy-based IPsec and we already have an IPsec profile that expects remote peer IPs and allows specific transform sets. Can your Transit Gateway-facing VPN be configured to present a fixed peer IP (i.e., the TGW or an appliance EIP)?
- For vendor allow-lists: we really need a small set (<= 6) of public IPs that represent all outbound traffic from the inference environment. Is it operationally realistic to route all outbound to a central NAT pair?
- Compliance: our SOC 2 auditor will want Flow Logs for all interfaces and retention for 90 days. Can you collect and provide VPC Flow Logs and show delivery to our S3 or to an auditor endpoint?

If those three can be satisfied, we're comfortable with the hybrid approach you proposed. Please include a short mutual action plan: who does what and estimated windows. We're targeting a pilot by 2027-05-20.

Alex

Subject: RE: Private deployment: connectivity options, egress IP stability requirement — proposed MAP and next steps

Alex / Priya / CloudOps —

Thanks — confirmed: Transit Gateway can terminate an AWS-managed IPsec VPN and you can point your Palo Alto at a single public peer IP (the TGW VPN endpoint or an appliance EIP) for policy-based IPsec. That will satisfy your firewall requirement.

On the egress IPs: yes — the pattern is to force all outbound traffic from the inference VPC across the Transit Gateway into a central egress VPC that performs SNAT using a small pool of EIPs. We typically size the NAT pair for HA (active/standby) and keep the EIP pool <= 6 for allow-listing.

Flow logs / compliance: we can enable VPC Flow Logs for the Redwood Private VPC, deliver to your S3 bucket (or ours with cross-account read), and provide a short playbook for auditors showing retention and ACLs. We'll include log delivery confirmation in the compliance checklist.

Attached is a short mutual action plan (mutual-action-plan-nimbus.docx) — summary below: 
- Week 0 (this week): agree topology (this thread) and finalize SOW. (Owner: Nimbus + Redwood Sales/Legal)
- Week 1: Redwood infra creates TGW + egress VPC + interface endpoints in staging. (Owner: Redwood infra)
- Week 2: Establish TGW VPN to Nimbus Palo Alto (owner: Nimbus CloudOps + Redwood infra)
- Week 3: Smoke tests: egress IP validation with vendor allow-listing + flow log delivery test. (Owner: joint)
- Week 4–6: Pilot validation, perf testing, SOC 2 artifact collection (Owner: joint)

Open items (we will cover on the architect call):
- Exact EIP count you need for vendor allow-lists. We recommend 2–4 per AZ pair for HA; please confirm.
- Whether you want a dedicated AWS account for Redwood infra for extra isolation (affects SOW & lead time).

If you confirm the EIP budget and preferred pilot start date (target 2027-05-20), I'll schedule the 45-min technical deep-dive with Karthik and Grace and circulate the SOW draft.

Thanks,
Jonas Weber
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
